CausalChain: Inflammatory signals in HCC -> Increased IL-6 production -> Activation of STAT3 in tumor cells -> STAT3-driven transcriptional upregulation of AFP -> Secreted AFP interacts with IL-6 receptor components and/or downregulates SOCS -> Enhanced IL-6/STAT3 signaling -> Promotion of cancer stem cell features, drug resistance, and immune evasion
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in hepatocellular carcinoma, inflammatory signals lead to IL-6 overproduction and STAT3 activation, which upregulates AFP expression. Contrary to its conventional role as a biomarker, AFP acts as an active modulator by either directly interacting with the IL-6 receptor complex or by suppressing SOCS-mediated inhibition, thereby establishing a positive feedback loop that further enhances IL-6/STAT3 signaling. This amplification of oncogenic signaling contributes to cancer stem cell traits, drug resistance, and immune evasion. We propose to test this hypothesis using state-of-the-art CRISPR screens, single-cell RNA sequencing, and structural proteomics (including cryo-EM and computational modeling) to delineate the molecular interactions between AFP and IL-6/STAT3 pathway components in different HCC microenvironments.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by robust inflammatory signaling and aberrant activation of the IL-6/STAT3 pathway, leading to aggressive tumor behaviors and therapy resistance. Traditionally, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) has been used solely as a diagnostic marker; however, emerging evidence suggests that AFP may function as an active modulator of this oncogenic cascade. Here, we propose a refined hypothesis in which inflammatory cues in HCC elevate IL-6 levels that activate STAT3, which in turn drives the transcriptional upregulation of AFP. Secreted AFP then acts in a context-dependent manner by either binding to components of the IL-6 receptor complex or by modulating inhibitory signals (such as SOCS proteins), thereby further amplifying IL-6/STAT3 signaling. By leveraging contemporary technologies—including CRISPR-based genetic screens, single-cell transcriptomics, and advanced proteomic mapping combined with structural bioinformatics—we aim to elucidate the putative AFP–IL-6/STAT3 positive feedback loop and determine its role in promoting cancer stem cell features, drug resistance, and immune evasion. This refined framework not only deepens our understanding of AFP’s functional role in HCC but also offers a potential therapeutic target for mitigating tumor aggressiveness through disruption of this feedback mechanism.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that AFP enhances IL-6/STAT3 signaling via a positive feedback loop in HCC, focusing on its role in promoting tumor aggressiveness and drug resistance. The revised hypothesis retains this causal chain but integrates contemporary technological approaches to test specific molecular interactions. Key modifications include: (1) detailing the context-dependent mechanisms by which AFP might interact with the IL-6 receptor complex or modulate SOCS proteins; (2) proposing the use of modern techniques such as CRISPR-based genetic screens, single-cell transcriptomics, and advanced structural proteomics to provide mechanistic insights; and (3) acknowledging potential compensatory pathways that could modulate the feedback loop, thereby strengthening the hypothesis’ logical coherence and experimental feasibility.
